# Choosing a Model {#sec-choosing-model}

Choosing a model for production means choosing a **versioned served system**:
a particular model revision, provider or serving build, prompt, tools,
settings, safety controls, and fallback behavior. A different prompt template
or tool loop can change the result even when the weights stay fixed, so a
leaderboard position, measured under the benchmark's own prompts, tools, and
settings, is only a starting point for the decision.

The selection starts from a **workload contract**, a written statement of which
tasks matter, what counts as an accepted result, which hard constraints apply,
and the limits for quality, cost, latency, availability, and operational risk.
Eligible candidates are then compared under that same contract. The comparison
supports a choice for the declared workload and time period only; there is no
universal winner across workloads.

This chapter turns that idea into a procedure and gives each step its current
material: the hosted families and the channels that sell them, open-weight
releases by hardware class, the public boards and what each can establish, an
evaluation contract, and a routing configuration. Where a release sits between
closed and open weights is one input to the procedure. How to inspect a
release is covered in @sec-model-landscape, and what a public score can and
cannot establish is covered in @sec-benchmarks.

## Identify the served system

A family name such as “Model Pro” is too vague to reproduce a result. Record
the exact candidate identity before testing it:

- provider and model ID, or artifact digest for downloaded weights;
- endpoint and region;
- prompt template and message formatting;
- tool schemas and tool-loop implementation;
- decoding and reasoning settings, including budgets and stopping rules;
- safety policy and content filters;
- cache, batch, router, and fallback policy; and
- rate and capacity limits used during the test.

Call this configuration $m$. If any behavior-changing field changes, the
changed configuration is a new candidate. The record carries a date even when
an API exposes a fixed-looking name, because service implementations, quotas,
and terms can change outside the repository.

Earlier work on evaluation and documentation already treats the conditions
around a model as part of what is reported. Liang and colleagues introduced
HELM in 2022 and published it in 2023 to compare language models across
scenarios and multiple metrics under standardized conditions
[@liang2023helm]. Mitchell and colleagues introduced model cards in 2019 so
that intended uses, evaluation conditions, and limitations travel with a model
release [@mitchell2019modelcards]. The served configuration that an application
calls can carry the same kind of card.

Fallback needs its own entry on that card, because it can change the served
model within one request. A gateway can retry a failed call on another provider.
Some providers also run safety classifiers on requests and responses and, when a
classifier refuses, can rerun the request on a different model billed at that
model's price. With fallback enabled, one configuration $m$ serves a mixture of
models, and its measured quality, cost, and refusal rate describe the mixture.
The card therefore states whether fallback is on and which models it can reach,
and each request logs the model that produced the answer, as the trace record in
the wiring section below requires. An evaluation can then report the primary
model and the fallback separately.

::: {.callout-note .dated}
## As of September 2026

Anthropic's Claude Fable 5, released in June 2026, runs safety classifiers on
requests and during response generation. When a classifier declines, the API
returns `stop_reason: "refusal"`, and an opt-in `fallbacks` parameter reruns the
refused request on another model, billed at that model's rates
[@anthropic2026releasenotes]. Published comparisons now mark such results as
run with fallback. Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 model card states that Fable 5 hit
fallbacks on 35 percent of the tasks in one of its coding evaluations, which may
have lowered its measured score [@moonshot2026kimik3card].
:::

Variant names inside a family can also change meaning. Providers reuse variant
words across generations, and the same word can name a different tier in the next
generation, with a different price and capability. A record or routing rule keyed
on the variant word alone can move to another class of model when a generation
ships; the full model ID and the observation date identify the candidate.

::: {.callout-note .dated}

A pinned model ID also has a limited lifetime. Providers retire models on a
published schedule, and two of its terms belong in the eligibility review: the
minimum notice before retirement, and what happens to requests afterward. Requests
to a retired model may fail, or the provider may redirect them to another model at
that model's price. A failure is visible at once. A redirect changes the served
system and the bill without any change to the application, and only the
per-request model log or a rerun of fixed test cases reveals it.

::: {.callout-note .dated}
## As of September 2026

Anthropic commits to at least 60 days' notice before retiring a publicly released
model; requests to a retired model fail, and Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud set
their own retirement schedules for the same models [@anthropic2026deprecations].
xAI retired several model identifiers, including `grok-4-1-fast-reasoning`, on
15 May 2026 and redirected their requests to `grok-4.3`, billed at `grok-4.3`
rates of $1.25 per million input tokens and $2.50 per million output tokens instead
of the original model's rates [@xai2026retirement].
:::

The selection then runs in a fixed order: freeze the workload contract, reject
ineligible systems at hard gates, measure the survivors with a paired
evaluation and a load test, remove dominated candidates, and roll out the
choice through shadow traffic and a canary. The order prevents an attractive
score from hiding a legal, interface, or capacity failure. It also prevents a
cheap but inadequate system from entering an economic comparison.

## Gate eligibility before ranking

Write hard requirements as predicates. For candidate $m$, one compact gate is

$$
E(m)=H_{\mathrm{license}}(m)
\land H_{\mathrm{data}}(m)
\land H_{\mathrm{region}}(m)
\land H_{\mathrm{interface}}(m)
\land H_{\mathrm{capacity}}(m).
$$

Here $H_{\mathrm{license}}(m)$ means the legal review permits the intended use;
$H_{\mathrm{data}}(m)$ means service handling and retention satisfy policy;
$H_{\mathrm{region}}(m)$ means deployment and processing locations are allowed;
$H_{\mathrm{interface}}(m)$ means required modalities, tools, and output forms
work; and $H_{\mathrm{capacity}}(m)$ means the candidate can meet the required
load and availability. Every factor is Boolean, and an unknown does not pass.
Eligibility is therefore not a weighted score: an unresolved item goes through
an explicit exception process instead of entering a score as a small penalty.

The gate should cover more than these five examples when the workload requires
it: accessibility, safety controls, export restrictions, audit evidence,
indemnity, data deletion, or an exit path can all be hard requirements.

Availability belongs in the gate as well. A model that leads a public board can
be withdrawn, restricted to some customers or regions, or rate-limited below
the required load, on a schedule the application's owner does not control. The
gate therefore admits only models that are available to the organization under
its own policies, and the selection keeps a fallback that passed the same gate
and the same evaluation. Losing the primary model then changes a routing rule
instead of stopping the product.

::: {.callout-note .dated}

### “Open” is not enough information

Keep the artifacts and the permissions in separate columns. A release may
provide weights without training data, training code, or a useful model card.
A permissive code license attached to one repository does not automatically
describe the terms for weights or data. A hosted service adds another contract
covering data retention, training on customer data, regions, acceptable use,
rate limits, deprecation, and support.

The Open Source Initiative's 2024 definition asks whether a system grants the
freedoms to use, study, modify, and share, and whether the preferred form for
modification includes the needed data information, code, and parameters
[@osi2024osaid]. That definition asks for more than downloadable weights. The
word open does not by itself establish any right, so each artifact, license,
and service agreement that applies to the exact deployment is inspected on its
own. This is an engineering review framework, not legal advice.

By their terms, current releases fall into three groups, and a release can sit
in a different group from others in its own family:

- **Permissive licenses.** Apache 2.0 and MIT grant use, modification, and
  redistribution without user caps or field-of-use limits. gpt-oss, Gemma 4,
  Qwen3.8-27B, and OLMo 3.1 use Apache 2.0 [@openai2025gptoss; @google2026gemma4;
  @qwen2026qwen3827b; @allenai2025olmo31think]; DeepSeek-V4 and GLM-5.3-Flash use
  MIT [@deepseek2026v4procard; @zai2026glm53flash].
- **Permissive grants with conditions.** Several 2026 flagships add a clause to
  an otherwise permissive grant, most often a separate agreement for companies
  that sell hosted access above a revenue threshold. The Qwen3.8 flagship, Kimi
  K3, and GLM-5.3 are in this group [@qwen2026qwen38max;
  @moonshot2026kimik3license; @zai2026glm53license]; @sec-model-landscape
  records each clause and its threshold.
- **Hosted only.** No weights are released, and the service agreement is the
  only contract. Most frontier hosted models are in this group.

A second distinction is independent of the license: whether a release ships
weights only or the full development stack. Most releases in the first two
groups publish weights, a model card, and inference code. OLMo 3.1 is trained on
Ai2's Dolma 3 corpus and ships with its code and intermediate checkpoints
[@allenai2025olmo31think]. When reproducibility, an audit of the training data,
or retraining from scratch is a requirement, only a release of the second kind
meets it.

### Hosted, managed, and self-hosted are deployment choices

Access to an artifact limits the deployment options without fixing one.
Downloadable weights can run on owned machines, rented accelerators, or a
managed endpoint. A hosted API can be reached directly or through a cloud
marketplace. Its service terms are distinct from an artifact license. Compare
the actual alternatives available to the organization, including their
capacity, staffing, security, and exit costs.

Renting and owning assign the serving work differently. Behind a hosted API,
the provider runs the serving system: batching, the @gls-kv-cache (the stored
keys and values of earlier tokens), speculative decoding, autoscaling, and the
accelerators (@sec-serving-stack). The application inherits the provider's
latency distribution and rate limits, and it reaches the serving optimizations
only through price terms such as cached-input rates, batch tiers, and priority
tiers. With downloaded weights, the team runs an inference server such as vLLM,
SGLang, or llama.cpp, and in exchange controls cost, latency, data residency,
and the right to fine-tune (@sec-training-practice). The model family then
fixes what that server must load and how much accelerator memory it needs.

A hosted family is often sold through several channels: the developer's own API
and one or more cloud marketplaces, where procurement, committed-use discounts,
regions, and data handling follow the cloud contract. The cloud an organization
already buys from is therefore a strong first filter. Each channel is a separate
candidate identity in the record above, because a marketplace can list
different versions and model IDs and sets its own retirement dates.

| Provider (family) | Weights | Channels | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **OpenAI** (GPT) | Hosted only; gpt-oss is its open-weight line | OpenAI API, Microsoft Azure, Amazon Bedrock | Higher rates above a prompt-length threshold |
| **Anthropic** (Claude) | Hosted only | Claude API, Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud, Microsoft Foundry | Every model ID is a pinned snapshot |
| **Google** (Gemini) | Hosted only; Gemma is its open-weight line | Gemini API, Google Cloud Vertex AI | Higher rates above a prompt-length threshold |
| **xAI** (Grok) | Hosted only | xAI API, Amazon Bedrock | The higher rate covers every token of a long request |
| **DeepSeek** | Open weights under MIT, plus a first-party API | DeepSeek API; the weights run anywhere | Peak and off-peak prices by time of day |
| **Mistral AI** | Open weights for Mistral Large 3 under Apache 2.0 | Mistral API, Amazon Bedrock | Also self-hostable, see the next table |
| **Amazon** (Nova) | Hosted only | Amazon Bedrock | Sold only through its own cloud |

### Open-weight releases by hardware class

For downloaded weights, the capacity predicate usually removes candidates
first, and it depends on total parameters and release precision more than on
benchmark rank. A @gls-moe model routes each token through a few of its expert
layers, so its per-token compute follows the active parameters while its memory
follows the total. The table lists releases from small to large with the size
of their published weight files and the smallest common accelerator
configuration whose memory holds those weights. The KV cache, activations, and
redundant replicas need memory beyond the weights, so a production host is
often one size larger, and a load test decides.

## Lower-layer constraint: production load shapes the shortlist

For a self-managed candidate, total parameters, precision, memory layout, and
runtime support determine whether the artifact fits at all. DeepSeek-V4-Pro in
the table above shows the effect: it activates 49B of its 1.6T parameters for
each token, so its per-token compute is close to that of a 49B dense model, yet
its weight files alone exceed the 640 GB of an eight-GPU node of 80 GB
accelerators before any KV cache is allocated. Production-shaped load tests then
determine capacity at the required tail latency and redundancy. Average tokens
per second on an idle server is not a capacity plan. The checks
that a hardware claim has to pass are covered in @sec-serving-stack and
@sec-quantization-kernels.
:::

## Use public evidence to discover candidates

Public benchmarks are useful for candidate discovery. They are weak grounds for
a production decision unless their task, system, and measurement process match
the production workload. HELM's scenario-and-metric framing is useful because it
makes those choices visible [@liang2023helm].

Four questions apply to every published result:

1. **Construct match:** does the benchmark measure the capability the product
   needs, or a convenient proxy?
2. **Harness match:** are the prompt, tools, sampling, context, budget, and
   grader comparable to production?
3. **Uncertainty:** are item counts, repeated runs, intervals, and close ranks
   reported well enough to support the claimed difference?
4. **Data provenance:** when and how were tasks created, exposed, filtered, and
   scored?

Each result also has to be tied to the system being measured. An agent
benchmark usually measures a model together with a scaffold (the surrounding
program that prompts the model and executes its tool calls), tools, retries,
and budget. SWE-bench, for example, evaluates issue resolution in real
repositories, not isolated code completion [@jimenez2024swebench]. LiveCodeBench continuously draws newer
competition problems and covers several coding behaviors
[@jain2024livecodebench]. These design choices address different questions;
neither score transfers automatically to a private workload.

Human-preference boards answer yet another question. Chatbot Arena uses paired
user preferences and a statistical ranking method [@chiang2024arena]. That is
evidence about aggregate preference under its traffic and interface, not direct
proof of factual correctness, policy compliance, or tool reliability.

Each kind of board answers one question, and reading several kinds narrows the
candidates better than any single rank. Agreement between boards that measure
different things is stronger evidence than a lead on one of them, and a
disagreement shows which property of the candidate is fragile.

| Question | Where to look | What it cannot establish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Do users prefer its answers in open-ended chat? | Chatbot Arena, paired human preferences [@chiang2024arena] | Correctness: a confident, longer, well-formatted answer can win while wrong |
| How much measured capability per dollar? | Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, one standardized harness with cost per task [@artificialanalysis2026solluna] | Whether that harness matches the production prompts, tools, and sampling |
| Does a score hold on tasks the model has not seen? | Refreshed or independently run sets: LiveCodeBench [@jain2024livecodebench], Epoch AI's benchmarking hub [@epoch2026gpqa], Scale's leaderboards [@scale2026hleleaderboard] | Broad coverage: these sets are smaller and update more slowly |
| Can it drive an agent loop? | Executable agent benchmarks: Terminal-Bench [@tbench2026v4], τ-bench [@sierra2026taubench100], BFCL for function calling [@patil2025bfcl], the SWE-bench family [@jimenez2024swebench] | Single-turn knowledge; the scaffold is part of the score (@sec-evaluating-agents) |
| Did a new version regress on basics? | Saturated suites such as MMLU [@hendrycks2020mmlu] and HumanEval [@chen2021humaneval], as a floor only | Frontier ranking: the leaders differ by noise |

::: {.callout-note .dated}
## As of September 2026

OpenAI no longer evaluates SWE-bench Verified: a re-audit of frequently failed
tasks found test and specification defects and signs that tasks had been
exposed [@openai2026swebenchverified]. Separately, repository maintainers who
reviewed agent patches that passed its tests would have rejected about half of
them [@metr2026swebenchmerge]. Terminal-Bench 2.1 fixed 28 tasks of version 2.0
and moved scores for the same agent and model by up to 12.1 points
[@tbench2026v21]. Terminal-Bench 4.0, released on 28 August 2026, removed eight
tasks, two of them because every latest-generation model solved them in five of
five attempts, and adopted semantic versioning [@tbench2026v4]. A score is
comparable only with scores from the same benchmark version.
:::

A suspicious gap between public and private results justifies investigation,
but the gap alone cannot prove contamination, the leakage of benchmark items
into a model's training data. Task mix, prompts, tools, budgets, graders, and
chance can also create the gap. Record the possible explanations and run
controlled tests instead of assigning a cause from one comparison.

::: {.callout-important}
## What's contested: one rank or a decision-relevant estimate?

Benchmark accuracy can mean performance on a fixed set or an estimate for a
larger population of similar tasks. Those targets require explicit assumptions
and can have different uncertainty. NIST's statistical treatment of language
model evaluation makes that distinction concrete [@keller2026nist]. A selection
review therefore states which target a reported accuracy refers to. A rank
supports a procurement decision only when it comes with a target population and
an uncertainty interval.
:::

### From constraints to a shortlist

Public evidence and the hard gate together produce a shortlist of three or four
candidates for the internal evaluation. The constraints usually decide in this
order, before quality does:

1. **Governance and residency.** A strict data-residency or sovereignty rule
   limits the candidates to providers with endpoints in the allowed regions, or
   to self-hosted weights.
2. **Rent or own.** Renting starts from the catalog of the channel the
   organization already buys through; owning starts from the hardware class in
   the table of open-weight releases above.
3. **Task shape.** Within what remains, the task decides which families to test
   first.

The examples below are candidates to test as of September 2026, not a ranking,
and each row changes with the next release.

| Task shape | Hosted candidates | Open-weight candidates |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Long-running agentic coding | Claude Opus 5.5 or Fable 5.1; GPT-6 Astra or GPT-6 Sol | GLM-5.3, Kimi K3, DeepSeek-V4-Pro |
| High-volume traffic under a cost cap | GPT-6 Luna, Claude Haiku 4.5, Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, DeepSeek's flash model | gpt-oss-120b, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash |
| Images, video, and long documents in one request | Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview | Kimi K3, Mistral Large 3 |

Two constraints map directly onto the hardware table. Self-hosting on one 80 GB
GPU per replica starts from the rows between Qwen3.8-27B and gpt-oss-120b. A
requirement for reproducible training or an audit of training data leaves OLMo
3.1 among the releases in the table. In every case the shortlist is the input to the
evaluation below, which makes the choice.

## Build the evaluation around the workload

The internal evaluation is the decision instrument. Its written plan, the
evaluation contract, is frozen before anyone looks at final results:

- define workload strata, such as language, task type, difficulty, risk, and
  input size, with production weights;
- write the acceptance rule and primary quality measure;
- name the incumbent baseline and the smallest practically important change;
- separate tuning cases from a locked confirmation set;
- declare cost, latency, critical-failure, and availability limits; and
- choose a precision target and sample size plan.

Run every candidate on the same cases. Randomize execution across time when
provider load may drift, and use repeated trials at production settings when
generation is stochastic. Preserve the independent unit: several turns from
one conversation or several attempts on one issue are clustered observations,
not unrelated evidence.

For a challenger $m$ and baseline $b$, define the paired result on independent
case $i$ as

$$
d_i = y_i^{(m)}-y_i^{(b)},
$$

where $y_i^{(m)}$ and $y_i^{(b)}$ are scores produced under the frozen
acceptance rule. Before running the comparison, choose a non-inferiority margin
$\delta>0$: the largest quality loss the team would accept for gains elsewhere.
The challenger clears the quality gate only when the lower bound of the
confidence interval for the workload-weighted mean difference is greater than
$-\delta$. Require a lower bound above zero if the claim is superiority.

The rule fixes the decision criterion; the interval method behind it depends on
the data. Binary paired outcomes, rubric scores, clustered conversations, and
repeated stochastic runs need different interval methods;
@sec-statistical-reliability develops those choices. Sample size follows from
the precision target, expected paired variance, cluster structure, and desired
error rates, so no fixed item count suits every evaluation. Inspect per-stratum
results and critical failures even when the aggregate passes.

The runnable below applies the rule to simulated results and shows why the
pairing matters. Each case has its own pass rate, shared by both systems, so
some cases are easy for both and others hard for both; the challenger is one
point worse on average, and the margin is five points. The paired bootstrap
resamples whole cases, which keeps each $d_i$ intact and cancels the shared
difficulty. The unpaired bootstrap resamples the two systems separately, as if
they had been run on different cases. On the same data, the paired interval
clears the margin with 200 cases, and the unpaired one needs several times as
many. Setting `a = 5` makes the cases similar in difficulty, and the advantage
of pairing nearly disappears.

:::: {.runnable}
```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
delta, R, B = 0.05, 3, 2000   # margin, repeats per case, bootstrap draws
a = 0.5                       # difficulty spread; small a: cases differ a lot

def bootstrap(n):
    p = rng.beta(a, a, n)                                   # pass rate of each case
    y_b = (rng.random((n, R)) < p[:, None]).mean(1)         # incumbent b
    y_m = (rng.random((n, R)) < p[:, None] - 0.01).mean(1)  # challenger m, 1 point worse
    i, j = rng.integers(0, n, (2, B, n))
    paired = (y_m[i] - y_b[i]).mean(1)          # resample cases, keeping each d_i whole
    unpaired = y_m[i].mean(1) - y_b[j].mean(1)  # resample the two systems separately
    return paired, unpaired

print(f"lower bound of the 95% interval; the gate needs > {-delta}")
for n in (50, 200, 800):
    paired, unpaired = bootstrap(n)
    lo = [np.percentile(s, 2.5) for s in (paired, unpaired)]
    print(f"n={n:4d}  paired {lo[0]:+.3f} {'pass' if lo[0] > -delta else 'fail'}"
          f"  unpaired {lo[1]:+.3f} {'pass' if lo[1] > -delta else 'fail'}")
print(f"unpaired interval / paired interval: {unpaired.std() / paired.std():.1f}x")
```
::::

Prefer executable or rule-based graders where they represent acceptance.
When human judgment is necessary, blind the reviewer to candidate identity and
randomize presentation order. When an LLM judge, a language model prompted to
grade outputs, is necessary, pin its full configuration, validate it against
human labels, measure judge disagreement, swap answer order, and adjudicate
important conflicts. LLM judges can exhibit position bias, favoring an answer
because of where it appears [@wang2024judges]; @sec-judging-holistic and
@sec-evaluating-agents cover the broader evaluation design.

A reviewable configuration might look like this:

```yaml
# eval-contract.yaml: illustrative fields, not universal thresholds
workload: evals/support-confirmation-v8.jsonl
strata: [language, request_type, risk, input_size]
candidate_systems:
  - config: systems/incumbent-2026-08-01.yaml
  - config: systems/challenger-a-2026-08-01.yaml
primary_metric: accepted_result
graders:                                  # executable wherever acceptance allows
  - type: exact_match
  - type: unit_test                       # for code-shaped outputs
  - type: llm_judge                       # only where no executable check exists
    judge: systems/judge-2026-08-01.yaml  # pinned model, prompt, and rubric
    validated_against: evals/human-labels-v3.jsonl
    swap_answer_order: true
comparison:
  design: paired
  repeats_per_case: 3
  noninferiority_margin: declared-before-run
  confidence_method: chosen-for-independent-unit
secondary_limits: [critical_failure_rate, cost_per_accepted_task, p95_latency]
release: [shadow, canary, rollback]
```

## Compare total cost for accepted work

Token price is one input to cost. Tokenizers, cache rules, reasoning tokens,
output length, tool use, retries, and acceptance rates also differ between
candidates, so the comparison measures end-to-end **cost per accepted task**
over the same accounting horizon and workload.

Here $s$ identifies a workload stratum and $r$ a repeated trial. Let $w_s$ be the
production weight of stratum $s$, $K_{msr}$ the realized end-to-end cost of
candidate $m$, and $A_{msr}$ equal one when the result is accepted and zero
otherwise. Then

$$
C_m=
\frac{\sum_s w_s\sum_r K_{msr}}
     {\sum_s w_s\sum_r A_{msr}}.
$$

$C_m$ is undefined when the weighted accepted count is zero, and that undefined
value signals a candidate with no accepted results. In this formula, the ledger
behind $K_{msr}$ should include input tokens, output tokens, cache writes and
reads, tool calls, retries, network charges, human review, and expected
incident cost. For self-managed serving it also includes accelerators,
CPU and memory, storage, idle capacity, operations labor, on-call work, and
software. Keep cost per attempt beside the accepted-task measure so a change in
the denominator remains visible.

Measure client-side latency as well. Report first-token and end-to-end p50, p95,
and p99 by workload stratum and offered load. Separate queueing, prefill,
decoding, tools, and retries when diagnosing the result. A routing cascade,
which sends a request to a cheaper model first and escalates it to a stronger
one when needed, can reduce average spend yet worsen the tail because
escalated requests pay for multiple stages.

Prompt length has its own price schedule. Several providers bill a request at a
higher rate once its prompt crosses a length threshold, and the higher rate
covers the whole request, so a prompt that grows past the threshold costs more
per token as well as for the added tokens. Retrieving a bounded slice of
evidence keeps prompts below the threshold and is usually cheaper than placing a
whole corpus in the context window (@sec-retrieval-practice). A check in the
gateway or client that flags requests near a threshold makes the tier visible
before the invoice does.

::: {.callout-note .dated}
## As of September 2026

OpenAI bills prompts above 272K input tokens at twice the input price and
one and a half times the output price: GPT-6 Sol goes from $2 and $10 per million
input and output tokens to $4 and $15 [@openai2026pricing]. Gemini 3.1 Pro
Preview costs $2 and $12 for prompts up to 200K tokens and $4 and $18 above
[@google2026geminipricing]. xAI bills Grok 4.7 at $2 and $6 below 200K prompt
tokens and at $4 and $12 for every token of a request whose prompt reaches that
threshold [@xai2026models]. DeepSeek prices by time of day instead: its
`deepseek-v4-pro` model costs $1.32 per million cache-miss input tokens and
$3.96 per million output tokens during weekday peak hours, and half that
off-peak [@deepseek2026pricing].
:::

### Hosted versus self-hosted crossover

For a quick sensitivity analysis, suppose two quality-equivalent alternatives
meet the same service objective. Over one accounting period, write

$$
C_h(N)=F_h+Nv_h
$$

where the subscript $h$ denotes hosted service, and

$$
C_s(N)=F_s+Nv_s
$$

for self-hosted service. $N$ is accepted tasks in that period; $F_h$ and $F_s$
are fixed costs; and $v_h$ and $v_s$ are variable costs per accepted task. Use
the same currency and the same accounting horizon for every term. When
$v_h>v_s$, the linear crossover is

$$
N^*=\frac{F_s-F_h}{v_h-v_s}.
$$

A positive crossover exists only when the numerator and denominator imply
$N^*>0$. Otherwise there is no positive crossover in this linear range.
Real systems add capacity steps, demand bursts, commitments, utilization,
migration costs, and changing prices, so a full analysis builds low, base, and
high scenarios with the method in @sec-economics. The shortcut is invalid when
the alternatives are not quality-equivalent or meet different service
objectives.

## Select from the Pareto frontier

After the hard gate and quality gate, the survivors are placed on a **Pareto
frontier**, the set of candidates that no other eligible candidate dominates. A
candidate is dominated when another eligible candidate is at least as good on
every decision-relevant measure and better on at least one; dominated
candidates are removed. The remaining trade-off may still require judgment: one
team may pay more for a lower critical-failure bound, while another may accept
slower responses for data residency.

Arbitrary normalized weights would hide that judgment, so the trade-off is
recorded explicitly with its owner, evidence, and expiry date. Research on
learned cascades shows that routing can improve a measured cost-quality
trade-off [@chen2023frugalgpt; @ong2024routellm], but a router is itself a
versioned system. Evaluate the policy end to end, including misroutes, verifier errors,
duplicate work, fallback latency, and side effects.

```{figure}
//| figure: selection-frontier
//| label: fig-model-frontier
//| fig-cap: "Nine illustrative candidates, not measurements of any product. The table applies the hard gate $E(m)$ first: a candidate with a failing predicate, or an unknown one such as D's license review, is removed before it is measured. The plot shows the rest by cost per accepted task $C_m$ and acceptance on the confirmation set, with the interval of the paired difference $\bar d$ from the incumbent I. A challenger passes the quality gate when its interval ends above the dashed floor, the incumbent's rate minus $\delta$, and drops out above the declared p95 limit. Survivors beaten on both axes turn gray; the staircase through the rest is the frontier, and its points form the shortlist."
```

## Wire the decision so it stays true

Put provider-specific behavior behind a provider adapter when the application
needs portability or centralized controls. A @gls-gateway, a routing and policy
layer for model calls, is one design option for shared keys, budgets,
observability, and routing. It also adds a dependency and cannot make providers
semantically identical.

An OpenAI-compatible transport usually covers only a common subset. Tool
semantics, structured output, tokenization, caching, streaming, multimodal
inputs, reasoning controls, and error behavior can still differ. A
policy-compatible fallback must satisfy the same data and regional rules, and
its behavior must be validated by the same evaluation contract. Test ambiguous
timeouts and action idempotency before enabling automatic failover. See
@sec-wiring-stack and @sec-reliability.

A routing configuration puts the per-task choices, the fallback chain, and the
long-context guard in one reviewable file. The shape below is illustrative;
@sec-wiring-stack shows how gateways express the same routing.

```yaml
# gateway routing (illustrative); every model is a pinned ID from a decision record
default: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5
routes:
  - match: {task: hard_agentic}          # the steps that justify a higher price
    model: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5
  - match: {task: multimodal}            # images, video, and documents in one request
    model: google/gemini-3.1-pro-preview
  - match: {task: bulk}                  # high volume under a cost cap
    model: openai/gpt-6-luna
fallbacks:                               # each target passed the same gate and evaluation
  anthropic/claude-opus-5-5: [openai/gpt-6-sol]
  openai/gpt-6-luna: [selfhosted/gpt-oss-120b]
limits:
  warn_prompt_tokens: 200000             # below the providers' long-context thresholds
```

```{dot}
//| label: fig-model-wiring
//| fig-cap: "Deployment wiring. Versioned configuration drives an adapter or gateway; telemetry feeds the evaluation gate, and only an approved configuration is promoted."
digraph {
  bgcolor="transparent";
  rankdir=TB;
  nodesep=0.18; ranksep=0.25;
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9, color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280", fillcolor="#f1ece1", margin="0.06,0.04"];
  edge [fontsize=9, fontname="Helvetica", color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280", arrowsize=0.55];

  app [label="Application"];
  config [label="Pinned system\nconfiguration"];
  adapter [label="Provider adapter\nor gateway"];
  endpoint [label="Approved\nendpoint"];
  telemetry [label="Task, cost,\nlatency, failures"];
  eval [label="Evaluation\nand release gate"];

  app -> adapter;
  config -> adapter;
  adapter -> endpoint;
  endpoint -> telemetry;
  telemetry -> eval;
  eval -> config [style=dashed, label="approve change"];
}
```

Pin stable revisions where the provider or artifact supports them. Otherwise
record the exact endpoint, region, configuration, and observation date, then
run sentinel evaluations frequently. A sentinel evaluation reruns a small fixed
set of cases, so a change in served behavior shows up as a change in results.
Store selected-model and route decisions with each trace so failures can be
attributed to the system that handled them.

Promote through shadow traffic, then a small canary with automatic rollback.
Monitor acceptance, critical failures, latency tails, spend, capacity, and
provider errors by stratum. Define every re-evaluation trigger in advance:
model or prompt change, price or terms change, new tool schema, workload drift,
quality drift, repeated capacity failures, or the decision record's expiry
date.

The output is a decision record: the workload contract, candidate identities,
eligibility evidence, evaluation results with uncertainty, cost ledger, Pareto
trade-off, rollout owner, rollback rule, and re-evaluation trigger. With that
record, the current choice can be explained, and it can be replaced when a
re-evaluation trigger fires.
